briefs.label: Morning Brief
briefs.title: Momentum Building: Michigan Operators Find Workarounds as DEA Pushes Schedule III Home
briefs.top: Michigan operators are adapting to the 24% wholesale tax with cost-sharing deals, hospitality buildouts, and bipartisan repeal momentum, while nationally the DEA's own closing brief now argues for Schedule III and Compass Pathways' psilocybin therapy edges toward an FDA decision. Consolidation and fast-track drug reviews are reshaping both plant medicine categories into real growth stories for operators willing to move.

local.text: A Muskegon development called Fields Cannary is targeting a fall opening for its retail cannabis dispensary, with a full-service restaurant to follow — a hospitality-forward format pushing further than most Michigan dispensaries have gone.

JARS Cannabis is buying its way into a much bigger footprint out west, announcing a deal to acquire Sonoran Roots and its eight Ponderosa brand dispensaries, which will soon make JARS the largest dispensary chain in Arizona — proof a Michigan-born operator can scale nationally even under state tax pressure.

Michigan weed prices have leveled out after three months of steady increases following the wholesale tax, with the average ounce at $59 in April, down slightly from $62 in March, and Rize, which operates three Upper Michigan locations, has managed to sustain growth by negotiating cost-sharing arrangements with suppliers, splitting the tax burden rather than absorbing it alone.

Relief momentum is building on two fronts: GOP gubernatorial nominee John James says he will seek to repeal or sharply reduce the state's 24% marijuana wholesale tax if elected, making the levy a central part of a broader cannabis policy platform, while Genesee County Sheriff Chris Swanson, a Democratic gubernatorial candidate, called the tax "not fair and equitable" and promised to work to repeal it — bipartisan cover operators can build on.

The fight isn't over: adult-use marijuana sales from January through April were lower than the same months in 2025 and 2024, with January recreational sales falling to $226.4 million, an 8.2% decline from a year earlier — but MiCIA's constitutional lawsuit and multiple legislative repeal bills (SB 810, HB 6224) keep a clear legal and political path open for relief.

national.text: Rescheduling is closer than ever: the DEA formally argued that marijuana should move from Schedule I to Schedule III in its final post-hearing brief, telling the court that cannabis no longer meets the statutory criteria for Schedule I, with the full transcript now public as a judge weighs a recommendation.

Psychedelic medicine hit a durability milestone: Compass Pathways announced 26-week results confirming COMP360's rapid onset and durable profile in nearly 600 patients, and a rolling New Drug Application submission with the FDA is underway, with final submission on track for Q4 2026.

The FDA is fast-tracking the category: the agency issued national priority vouchers to three companies studying psilocybin for treatment-resistant depression, psilocybin for major depressive disorder, and methylone for PTSD, a pilot designed to compress review timelines dramatically.

Regulatory infrastructure is catching up: the FDA announced a public hearing on psychedelic therapeutic use scheduled for September 14, 2026, signaling the agency is building institutional groundwork for a live approval docket, after finalizing clinical trial guidance addressing the blinding issues that sank Lykos's 2024 MDMA bid.

Consolidation keeps rolling: Vireo Growth completed its acquisition of 17 PharmaCann Colorado retail dispensaries for approximately $49.0 million, expanding its Colorado retail footprint to 56 locations, while Grown Rogue International is acquiring PharmaCann's New York cannabis license and assets through a joint venture for an estimated $4.5 million.
